title: Round it, export it, compare it: the checks that remain after the model is trained
summary: The last Playground slides turn from training to use: rounding weights to a grid, exporting a rate network without its solver, changing one layer at a time, and keeping the comparison honest. The chart gives one concrete test: roll the whole trajectory out again after the change.

media.alt: Line chart titled check the entire rollout after rounding weights. Horizontal axis dimensionless time 0 to 4, vertical axis state y from 0 to 1.2. A black exact reference, a dashed orange curve for float weights and a dotted blue curve for 8-bit-grid rounded weights all follow the same decaying path from 1.2 to about 0.07 and cannot be told apart by eye.

read_the_figure.question: After the change (rounding, export, one modified layer), does the whole rollout still match, and what was held fixed?
read_the_figure.axes: Quantization chart: dimensionless time 0 to 4 against state y. Diagram slides: boxes in order of work: rate graph (ONNX candidate), host solver and scaling, rollout verify and time; baseline, one change, compare; microphones (loss signals), knobs (design choices), landscape (optimization).
look_at: Three curves on top of each other: no visible difference between float and rounded weights for this toy. That is a visual check only; the difference should be printed as a number.

Slide 33 diagram: the exported object is the rate graph only; the host provides the solver and the scaling; the rollout is then verified and timed. The caption says exporting the network alone does not export the solver.
Slide 34 diagram: baseline, one change, compare; keep the physical metric and the comparison budget explicit.
Slide 35 diagram: the course's three threads: microphones (the loss signals), knobs (design choices), landscape (optimization); the caption asks which part changes and what evidence shows it helps.
In every case the check is on the full rollout, not on one step.
read_the_figure.proves: A change is safe if the full rollout after the change agrees with the reference within a stated tolerance, with the solver, step size and scaling held fixed. A one-step error can look small and still accumulate.
if_wrong: A rounded model that agrees at the first step but not at the end: errors accumulate along the rollout.
An exported network used with a different solver or step: you have a different model.
Two things changed at once: no attribution is possible.
A comparison with different budgets: the better method may just have had more.
must_check: That the solver, step size and scaling are identical before and after the change.
That the rollout error is printed with its tolerance.
That one change is made at a time.
That the metric and budget of the comparison are stated.

terms.meaning: Replacing real-valued weights by values on a coarse grid, for example 256 levels for 8 bits.
A portable file format for a computation graph; it carries the network, not the integration method.
The numerical integrator that calls the exported rate graph at deployment.
A comparison in which exactly one component is changed.
The compute, data and tuning effort allowed to each variant.

remember: Rounding error per weight is at most half a grid step.
Errors in a rate propagate through the whole rollout; check the full trajectory.
The solver is part of the model you run; export and test it too.
Change one thing at a time and keep the metric and budget fixed.
A print of the largest difference beats an overlay of curves.

steps.note: L is the Lipschitz constant of the rate. For a contracting toy like this decay, L is small or negative and the curves stay together; for an unstable or stiff problem the bound grows quickly.

worked.title: Rounding error of an 8-bit grid
worked.problem: Weights lie in [-1, 1]. Find the grid step and the largest rounding error of a weight.
worked.answer: Step about 0.0078, largest error about 0.0039 per weight.

checks.q: What is exported in an ONNX rate graph?
checks.answer: The network that computes the rate, not the solver or the scaling.

checks.q: Why can a small one-step error produce a large rollout error?
checks.answer: Errors enter at every step and can be amplified by the dynamics; the bound grows like exp(L t).

checks.q: What would make a 'one change' comparison dishonest?
checks.answer: Different data, different solver or step size, different tuning effort, or a second change hidden in the first.

checks.q: Write the one sentence that the final slide's three boxes should be answered with for a new project.
checks.answer: 'We changed X (loss, design or optimizer) with Y held fixed, and the rollout metric Z moved by W over S seeds.'
